sourceDocuments.title: Interal grammar
sourceDocuments.scope: word formation, endings, suffixes, prefixes, and modified de Wahl rule

sourceDocuments.title: Interal semantic transparency document
sourceDocuments.scope: logical vs international derivative meanings and lexicalization risks

purpose.task: Evaluate whether an Interal candidate form can be accepted for a word that failed the five main lexical selection procedures.
important: Do not calculate numeric scores or percentages in the UI.
Use these rules as binding background for qualitative analysis.
Focus on future derivational potential, compatibility with Interal morphology, and risks of semantic opacity or conflict.

coreEvaluationQuestions: Can the candidate form generate useful nouns, adjectives, verbs, and abstract/action/result derivatives without excessive distortion?
Does the candidate form fit Interal word endings and ordinary spelling/phonological patterns?
If the form is or can become a verb, does it fit the modified de Wahl derivation logic?
Does the candidate create ambiguous or conflicting logical vs international meanings?
Does the form require marking with -u or a special adjective suffix to separate international meaning from logical meaning?
Can the candidate support derivatives by regular suffixes/prefixes without producing unnatural, misleading, or hard-to-learn forms?
Does the form avoid collisions with existing Interal forms or predictable forms created by regular rules?

notes: A noun can be formed from a verb in several equal ways, e.g. nomin(ar) -> nomina, nomin, nomine.
The ending -u is not a normal replaceable noun ending; it marks international meaning in certain double-meaning derivatives and must not be dropped when adding suffixes.
For living beings: -o masculine, -a feminine, -e neutral; a form without ending may also be neutral.
Plural is -(e)s: -es after consonants; -s after vowels and final c.

adjectives.defaultFormation: Adjectives can be formed with suffixes -al, -ari, -ic, -osi, -in, -aci, -esc, -ori, -id, -il, -inal, or by adding -i / no ending when suffix choice is uncertain.
notes: Because adjective suffix meanings overlap, -i or zero ending may replace a suffix if the naturalized suffix would be uncertain.
International adjective meanings often keep natural suffixes such as -al, -ari, -ic; logical adjective meanings can use -i.

verbs.infinitive: Infinitive adds -r; before -r the stem normally has -a, -e, or -i: crear, comprender, audir. Some roots use -n plus -a: printan, manajan, drinkan.
verbs.present: Present tense removes -r or -n from infinitive.
verbs.past: Past adds -t to present or uses did.

modifiedDeWahlRule.warning: The modified de Wahl rule must not be applied as blind string replacement only. The evaluator must check the natural derivative theme, consonant compatibility, and whether a conservative or modified root is required for logical vs international meaning.
scope: Use for deriving nouns/adjectives and suffixal derivatives from verbs, especially with suffixes -ion, -iv, -or, -oria, -ori, -ura, -al and some noun/adjective formations.
Use for Alter vordes when checking whether a candidate can function as a verb or generate a derivational family.

baseRules.operation: remove -er and add the required suffix; then apply final-root transformations below if relevant
remove -an and add the required suffix

baseRules.condition: After removing -er the root ends in a vowel
After removing -er the root ends in c or x or p
baseRules.operation: keep the consonant and add -t before the suffix

baseRules.condition: After removing -er the root ends in d
After removing -er the root ends in r
After removing -er the root ends in consonant + g
After removing -er the root ends in b
After removing -er the root ends in vowel + g, or h, or y

baseRules.operation: remove final -r and replace it with -t

alternativeForms.principle: Root-changing rules may be avoided in practice by using alternative forms based on the derived/perfect theme. Exceptions and alternative forms are equivalent.

notes: Root change or -t insertion applies only with suffixes -ion, -iv, -or, -oria, -ori, -ura, -al.

Root change or -t insertion also applies when forming a noun by adding -e or zero ending, or an adjective without suffix: morir -> mort(e), dictar -> dictate/dicta/dict(e), formar -> formate/forma/form(e), sentir -> sens(e), reger -> rect(i).
If an -er verb has a vowel-final root, the noun is formed by removing -er and adding -t: instituer -> institut.
If an infinitive ends in -an, noun formation replaces -an by -e or removes it; final -n is not simply removed: printan -> printe/print, flexan -> flexe/flex.

Nouns from verbs whose roots end in d or r preferably use the present theme, but the perfect theme is allowed: responder -> respond(e)/respons(e), seder -> sede, referer -> refer, transferer -> transfer.
-t and -an may be added to verbs ending in -ar and -ir: moderar -> moderatan, finir -> finitan.
Avoid forms that create confusion, e.g. dicta from dicter can be confused with dictar -> dicta.
Prefixed verbs derived from exception verbs inherit the exception.

byRoot: One-root verbs: end in -ar, -ir, or -er when the root ends in t or s, except -mitter and sentir; examples: combinar -> combinat-, audir -> audit-, posser -> poss-, constructer -> construct-.

Two-root verbs: -er verbs with present theme ending in c, g, b, p, d, r plus -mitter and sentir; examples: ducer -> duct-, ager -> act-, scriber -> script-, receper -> recept-, responder -> respons-, adherer -> adhes-, -mitter -> miss-, sentir -> sens-.
byForm: Two forms for one-root verbs: calcular -> calculatan, finir -> finitan, posser -> possan.

Three forms for two-root verbs: facer -> facter -> factan, reger -> recter -> rectan, absorber -> absorpter -> absorptan, caper -> capter -> captan, tender -> tenser -> tensan, currer -> curser -> cursan.

generalWordFormation.aprioriDerivatives: Words are formed by Interal rules, so apriori derivatives created inside word formation are allowed.
generalWordFormation.adjectiveSuffixWarning: When adjective suffixes such as -al, -ic, -ari are used, the specific suffix often must be learned; if uncertain, use -i instead.

compounds.rule: Compound words are formed by simple fusion of words; the head is at the end.
linkingVowels: -i may be inserted if the first root adds -ir to form a verb; otherwise use -o
compounds.hyphen: A hyphen may be used between words.

doubleMeaningAndSemanticTransparency.principle: Derivatives can have both a logical/compositional meaning and an international/naturalized meaning. These must be separated when ambiguity is significant.

diagnostics.predictability: Can the accepted meaning be inferred from components and Interal rules without prior knowledge?
diagnostics.relationality: Is there a semantic relation between the logical component meaning and the international meaning?
diagnostics.chainComplexity: How many semantic steps are needed from logical meaning to accepted/international meaning?
diagnostics.externalKnowledgeDependence: Does comprehension require history, idiom, traditional usage, or field-specific knowledge?

markingRules: Adjectives with international meaning receive a natural suffix such as -al, -ari, -ic; adjectives with logical meaning use -i.
Verbs and some nouns with international meaning keep the conservative root without adding/changing final root letters, e.g. obseder, projecer.
Verbs with logical meaning use the modified root basis, e.g. obsesser, projecter.
If there is no double root basis, one verb may carry both meanings, or the international verb can use suffix + -ar, e.g. repetitionar.
Endings used to distinguish meanings cannot be replaced by -e: projectu cannot become projecte, while project can.
When affixes are added to irregular derivatives, the meaning is the sum of the affix and the irregular derivative, unless an exception is specified.

examples.logical: obsession = sitting/opposite session; obsesser = sit opposite
repetition = repeated request; repetir = request again/rehearse

alterVordesUse: For Alter vordes, do not introduce a form that will create unresolved logical vs international ambiguity.
If a candidate naturally invites a logical derivative but the target meaning is internationalized, use the appropriate marking strategy or require manual review.
Prefer a form whose future derivative family remains interpretable or whose opacity is explicitly manageable.

suffixInventory.selectionRule: If a suffix varies by Romance infinitive endings (-ar, -er, -ir), forms beginning with a are used for -an infinitives: -antia, -anda, -ada, -ant, -abil.

nounSuffixes.notes: After t or s use -or with -er verbs.

nounSuffixes.meaning: person occupied with or possessing something
made of/consisting of/having character; collection; unit of measurement
movement, doctrine, religion, abstract concept or result

nounSuffixes.notes: After t and s use -oria, except -an verbs.

nounSuffixes.meaning: necessity/obligation to be or undergo something

nounSuffixes.notes: i -> e if root ends in i before suffix; if root ends in -er, add only -ta; adjective suffixes may optionally be retained before -ita.
Prefer with -o or -a to avoid confusion with adjective.

examples: italian = Italian language; italan = inhabitant of Italy

nounSuffixes.notes: Remove only -r or -n; if two vowels remain after removing -r, drop the last one.
When the same spelling has multiple suffix meanings, -e may distinguish one meaning.
i -> e if root ends in i before suffix.

verbSuffixes.notes: Both suffixes may be used equivalently with the same root.

generalNotes: A hyphen after a prefix is optional unless needed to separate meanings, e.g. ex- as former.
Prepositions may also be used as prefixes.
Check semantic scope carefully: some prefixes have multiple meanings and can create double meanings.

prefixes.notes: Do not use in- as opposite if it can be understood as 'in'; use des- instead.

prefixes.meaning: former when hyphenated; out/from when unhyphenated
separation/disconnection; can also be opposite meaning
opposite, in front of, against, near

scientificPrefixes.meaning: International System prefixes such as kilo-, hecto-, nano-, mega-

doubleConsonants.rule: Double consonants may be shortened in writing, e.g. grammatica -> gramatica.
doNotShortenIf: words differ only by doubled consonant and have different meanings, e.g. coma vs comma
the two letters are pronounced differently, e.g. success

rootReduction.rule: In many international word formations, two similar adjacent sounds or sound groups may reduce to one.
rootReduction.choice: Both reduced and unreduced forms may be used.

naturalisticAssimilation: con/in: col-/il- before l; cor-/ir- before r; com-/im- before p or m; co- before vowel and h.
ex: em- before m; el- before l.
sub: sup- before p; su- before s.
ad: at- before t; ac- before c; an- before n; ag- before g; al- before l; af- before f; as- before s; ar- before r.
ob: op- before p; of- before f.
dis: dif- before f; di- before g, l, m, r, v.
trans: tra- before d and j; tran- before s.
prefixAssimilation.note: Regular alternatives may be used alongside more naturalistic assimilated forms.

eligibleTrueWhen: The candidate is reasonably pronounceable and graphically compatible with Interal.
The candidate can form the relevant part-of-speech derivatives without severe ambiguity.
Future derivations by Interal suffixes/prefixes remain learnable and not misleading.
The candidate does not create serious unresolved logical vs international meaning conflict.
If a conflict exists, there is a clear Interal marking strategy such as -u, -i, or a natural adjective suffix.
eligibleFalseWhen: The candidate cannot support expected derivatives for its intended lexical family.
The candidate violates or strongly conflicts with modified de Wahl logic when used as or derived from a verb.
The candidate creates serious homonymy or semantic opacity without a marking strategy.
The candidate requires excessive historical/etymological knowledge for ordinary interpretation.
The candidate is too short or unstable to accept suffixes/prefixes clearly.
The candidate would collide with an existing or predictable Interal form.
needsManualReviewWhen: The candidate is usable only under a specific interpretation.
The candidate may require a double-form strategy but the correct distinction is unclear.
Qwen cannot determine whether the international or logical meaning should dominate.
There is insufficient information about existing Interal roots or expected derivative family.

do: Return qualitative analysis, not numeric scoring.
Mention which derivation rules were relevant.
Explain whether the candidate can form noun/adjective/verb derivatives.
Explain any modified de Wahl compatibility issue.
Explain if -u, -i, -al, -ari, -ic or another marking is needed.
Mark eligible false if derivational risks are serious.
doNot: Do not invent new Interal rules.
Do not treat Qwen's recommendation as final human decision.
Do not accept a form only because it is short; derivative compatibility is required.
Do not ignore logical vs international meaning conflicts.
